report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that drinking boiled garlic water *cures* COVID-19 is not supported by reliable clinical evidence.

**Why the idea may seem plausible:** Garlic contains organosulfur compounds with reported antiviral and immune-related activity. A scientific review describes these findings, but it is largely based on laboratory, animal, and non-COVID viral research—not evidence that garlic water treats SARS‑CoV‑2 infection in people. Boiling also changes garlic’s chemical composition, so evidence about garlic extracts or compounds would not establish efficacy for boiled water.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32836826/

**Evidence against the cure claim:** Reports promoting garlic as a COVID cure have been traced to *in-vitro* (test-tube) findings; experts note these do not demonstrate a treatment effect in humans, and prior clinical trials did not show garlic improved COVID recovery.  
https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/garlic-covid-cure-claim-crushed-by-experts/

By contrast, CDC guidance identifies tested antiviral treatments for eligible people at risk of severe disease, including nirmatrelvir–ritonavir (Paxlovid) and remdesivir; these need to be started promptly after symptoms begin. Garlic water is not among recommended COVID-19 treatments.  
https://www.cdc.gov/covid/treatment/index.html

Garlic used as food is generally fine for most people, but it is not risk-free in large or supplemental amounts: it can cause gastrointestinal symptoms or allergy, and supplements can increase bleeding risk—important for people taking anticoagulants.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/garlic

Do not substitute garlic water for medical care. If someone has COVID-19 and is older, immunocompromised, pregnant, or has chronic conditions, they should contact a clinician quickly to ask about antiviral eligibility; seek urgent care for trouble breathing, persistent chest pain, confusion, or inability to stay awake.
